evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

contextual_issues: Potential additional loss in salary beyond the counted sick-leave hours, depending on employment status and duration of absence, is mentioned by the authors but not separately quantified.

Hospital cost supplements (e.g., single-room upgrades, food, ambulance transport) and other non-reimbursed hospital costs are acknowledged as real but could not be captured because this information was not available in the MCD-MFD registry data.
Costs of prophylactic (post-tick-bite) antibiotic treatment are explicitly excluded from the analysis entirely.
Ambulatory laboratory tests other than LB serology, and medical acts for emergency-department visits, are mentioned as omitted from the direct medical cost estimate.

Caregiver/family burden for children is addressed only through an assumption (one parent takes sick leave during a child's hospitalization) built into the hospitalization productivity-loss calculation; children were excluded entirely from the ambulatory cohort, so pediatric at-home caregiving burden is not measured.

Possible over-use of LB serological testing without clear benefit to patient management is raised as a concern but not developed into a distinct burden estimate beyond the aggregate testing cost figure.

PTLDS subgroups in the cohort were very small (6 EM and 3 disseminated/late LB patients meeting the full IDSA PTLDS case definition), so PTLDS-specific cost estimates carry high uncertainty; the authors explicitly call for further research into PTLDS costs.

The incidence estimate (2015-2017 average) used to extrapolate costs nationally carries its own stated limitations from the source study (Geebelen et al. 2019), including a suspected underestimation of disseminated/late LB manifestations, which the current authors say could mean national costs for that group are themselves underestimated.

Quality of the ICD-10-CM hospital coding used to identify LB hospitalizations could not be checked, and there is no dedicated ICD-10-CM code for EM or PTLDS, so hospital-attributable costs for these subgroups cannot be separated from the disseminated/late LB hospitalization cost.

Patient/advocate audiences could use the patient-borne cost figures (out-of-pocket medical costs, all direct non-medical costs, and lost income) to illustrate that even in a largely reimbursed system, patients still carry a meaningful share of the burden. All of this applies specifically to the Belgian health system and 2019 euro price year and should not be transposed directly to other countries' dollar costs without explicit conversion and adjustment for differing case-mix and pricing, as the document itself flags when discussing non-comparability with US and other European cost studies.
use_cases: Policy analysts comparing the estimated €5.59 million/year Belgian national LB cost baseline against the projected cost of a prevention intervention (e.g., tick-bite prevention campaigns or a future vaccine) in a cost-effectiveness or budget-impact scenario.

Care delivery teams and clinicians using the EM-vs-disseminated/late-LB per-patient cost contrast (€193 vs €5,148) to motivate faster recognition and treatment of early-stage Lyme disease as an economically high-value early intervention point.

Patient advocates or payers illustrating that despite 75.5% of direct medical costs being reimbursed, patients still bear out-of-pocket medical costs, all direct non-medical costs (travel, paid help), and potential lost income, to inform discussions about remaining financial burden on patients.

spec.title: Belgian Lyme Disease (Borreliosis) Cost Burden Simulator
spec.boundary: Models the Geebelen et al. 2022 Belgian cost-of-illness estimate for Lyme borreliosis, comparing early-stage (erythema migrans) and disseminated/late-stage disease costs, covering direct medical, direct non-medical, and productivity-loss costs captured within roughly 6-12 months of diagnosis, in 2019 euros. It does not capture costs beyond that follow-up window, prophylactic treatment, non-reimbursed hospital supplements, pediatric at-home caregiving, or costs specific to post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome (PTLDS), all of which the source study flags as likely underestimated. Figures apply specifically to the Belgian health system and should not be converted directly to other countries' costs.

takeaway.patient: For a typical patient in this Belgian study, an early-stage Lyme rash (erythema migrans) cost about 193 euros on average, while disseminated or late-stage Lyme disease cost about 5,148 euros on average - roughly 26 times more. Even though most direct medical costs were reimbursed by insurance (about 75.5%), patients still paid a documented out-of-pocket share directly: about 23% of the early-stage total and about 6% of the late-stage total came straight out of patients' own pockets, on top of travel and other non-medical costs.
takeaway.care: This study found a roughly 26-fold gap in average per-patient cost between early-stage (erythema migrans) and disseminated/late-stage Lyme disease, with late-stage disease driving the majority of total cost despite being far less common. The study also notes that hospital billing data used no dedicated diagnostic code for erythema migrans or post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome, so all hospital-attributed costs were lumped into the disseminated/late-stage category regardless of the patient's actual presentation.
takeaway.policy: The study estimates Belgium's total annual cost of clinically manifest Lyme borreliosis at about 5.59 million euros (2019 euros), with disseminated/late-stage disease accounting for about 62% of that total despite being the less common manifestation. About 75.5% of direct medical costs were reimbursed by health insurance, leaving a documented non-reimbursed share; the authors explicitly flag this total as likely an underestimate because it excludes costs beyond 6-12 months, prophylactic treatment, and several non-reimbursed hospital cost categories.

patient: If you notice a tick bite or an early rash, consider seeking prompt medical evaluation - this study found early-stage Lyme disease cost patients and the health system far less than disease caught at a later, disseminated stage.

If you're billed for care related to Lyme disease, know that a non-reimbursed, out-of-pocket portion is a documented part of typical costs in this study (not unique to your situation) - it may be worth asking your insurer what portion of your bill is reimbursable.

If you develop disseminated or late-stage symptoms, keep track of your own travel and incidental expenses, since this study found these patients reported notably higher direct non-medical costs than early-stage patients.
care: This finding on the cost gap between early and late-stage disease may be worth checking against your own referral and testing pathway, to see whether diagnostic delay could be shifting patients into the costlier disseminated/late-stage category documented here.

The study's note that hospital billing codes cannot distinguish erythema migrans or post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome from disseminated/late Lyme disease may be worth raising with those responsible for your coding and documentation practices, since it limits what administrative cost data can tell you about these specific presentations.
Consider whether your current patient education or follow-up protocols for tick bites support earlier recognition of erythema migrans, given the scale of the documented cost difference.
policy: Use the approximately 5.59 million euro/year Belgian national cost estimate (2019 euros) as a baseline comparator when modeling the budget impact of prevention campaigns or a future Lyme vaccine.
Consider whether the 62% cost share attributable to disseminated/late-stage disease supports prioritizing investment in earlier-detection or public-awareness initiatives for erythema migrans.

When building any cost-effectiveness model from this baseline, account for the study's own stated gaps (costs beyond 6-12 months post-diagnosis, PTLDS-specific costs, prophylactic treatment) rather than treating the 5.59 million euro figure as a complete national cost.

package.documentation:
This simulator is based on Geebelen et al. 2022 (BMC Public Health), a Belgian cost-of-illness study of Lyme borreliosis combining a prospective outpatient cohort (HUMTICK, 2016-2020) with national hospital registry data (2016-2018), with all costs expressed in 2019 euros.

**Inputs:** Per-patient cost means for early-stage erythema migrans (EM) and disseminated/late-stage disease come directly from Table 4 (p.7). Patient out-of-pocket cost components come from the Discussion (p.8). The national total annual cost and the 62% cost share for disseminated/late disease come from the Abstract and Results (p.7). The direct-medical reimbursement rate (75.5%) comes from Results/Discussion (p.7-8). Several slider ranges (e.g., the national total's exploration band, the disseminated/late cost share's 50-75% band, and the per-patient cost bands) are assumed exploration bounds chosen partly to preserve the study's own early-vs-late cost ordering, not ranges stated by the source.

**Limitations:** Hospital costs were identified using ICD-10-CM billing/financing codes; the document states coding quality could not be verified and that this coding system "was not necessarily developed for surveillance purposes," so the hospital-cost component may undercount or misclassify true costs. There is no dedicated ICD-10-CM code for EM or for post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome (PTLDS), so hospital costs truly attributable to these presentations could not be separated from the disseminated/late LB group - a gap in the diagnostic-coding system itself, not just this study's analysis. The pooled per-patient and national totals shown here are not broken down by sex, age, or race/ethnicity, and the document does not report whether burden differs by these groups; federal survey sources (e.g., MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS) generally support disaggregated analysis of this kind even though this document did not perform it. The study also excludes costs beyond roughly 6-12 months post-diagnosis, prophylactic treatment, and many non-reimbursed hospital supplement costs, so the true annual burden may be higher than the reported national total. PTLDS-specific subgroup figures (as few as n=3 patients) carry high uncertainty and should not be treated with the same confidence as the main EM and disseminated/late-stage estimates. Costs from other European or US Lyme disease studies cited for context are explicitly stated by the authors to not be comparable to these Belgian figures and are not included in this simulator.
